hook: The atmosphere holds about 3,300,000,000,000,000 kg of carbon dioxide. A soil sample might hold 0.000002 g of a pesticide. Numbers this big and this small are hard to read and easy to miscopy, and on the exam a dropped zero costs the point. Scientific notation and metric prefixes keep them short and safe.

prereq.q: Which is an abiotic factor of an ecosystem?
Which biome is warm all year and very wet?
prereq.why: Warm and wet all year is a tropical rainforest.

figure.caption: Metric prefixes, their powers of ten and scale words.

chain.cause: Move the decimal point until one nonzero digit is left of it
chain.effect: the front number is between 1 and 10

chain.cause: Count the places you moved it
chain.effect: that count is the exponent: left gives a positive power, right a negative one
multiply the front numbers and add the exponents

ideas: Scientific notation writes a number as (a number from 1 to 10) × a power of ten: $2.5 \times 10^{6}$ = 2.5 million = 2,500,000.
Multiply: multiply the fronts, add the exponents. Divide: divide the fronts, subtract the exponents. Then fix the front number if it is not between 1 and 10.
A metric prefix is a power of ten: kilo ($10^{3}$), mega ($10^{6}$), giga ($10^{9}$), centi ($10^{-2}$), milli ($10^{-3}$), micro ($10^{-6}$).
Scale words: thousand = $10^{3}$, million = $10^{6}$, billion = $10^{9}$, trillion = $10^{12}$.

misconception.wrong: When you multiply $10^{4}$ by $10^{3}$, you multiply the exponents to get $10^{12}$.
misconception.right: Multiplying powers of ten adds the exponents: $10^{4} \times 10^{3} = 10^{7}$. Check with numbers: 10,000 × 1,000 = 10,000,000, which has 7 zeros.

summary: Scientific notation writes very large and very small numbers as a number from 1 to 10 times a power of ten, such as $2.5 \times 10^{6}$ = 2.5 million = 2,500,000. To multiply, multiply the fronts and add the exponents; to divide, divide and subtract. Metric prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro) are powers of ten too, so change them before you compare or combine numbers.
